replacement: Plans had been settled between the Athenians and their correspondents, both for what was to be said and for what was to be done. The Athenians then sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under Hippocrates, and took post in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be dug for the walls. Demosthenes, the other commander, placed himself in ambush with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it that night except those whose business it was to know. A little before daybreak the traitors in Megara began to act. For a long time they had been in the habit, every night, of carrying a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and sailing out in it, under pretense of marauding. This gave them a means of opening the gates, and they did it with the consent of the officer in command. They brought the boat back on the cart before day and took it inside the wall through the gates. Their pretended aim was to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbor. On this occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat. The Athenians, who had agreed on this with the traitors, saw it and ran from the ambush at top speed, to reach the gates before they were shut again and while the cart was still there to keep them from closing. At the same moment their Megarian accomplices killed the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, at the very spot where the trophy now stands. He was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and so secured the gates for the Athenian heavy infantry coming up.

note: Parentheses around "he had marched out by night" dropped; "Their purpose" wrongly reads as the Athenians' (Brasidas's purpose).
replacement: Just at this time the Lacedaemonian Brasidas, son of Tellis, happened to be in the neighborhood of Sicyon and Corinth, getting ready an army for Thrace. As soon as he heard that the walls had been taken, he feared for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and for the safety of Megara. He sent to the Boeotians to meet him as quickly as possible at Tripodiscus, a village of the Megarid so called, under Mount Geraneia. He went there himself with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian heavy infantry, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and such troops of his own as he had already levied, expecting to find Nisaea not yet taken. Hearing of its fall (he had marched out by night to Tripodiscus), he took three hundred picked men from the army without waiting until his coming should be known, and came up to Megara unobserved by the Athenians, who were down by the sea. His purpose was, ostensibly, and really if possible, to make an attempt on Nisaea, but above all to get into Megara and secure the town. He accordingly invited the townspeople to admit his party, saying that he had hopes of recovering Nisaea.

note: Serial verbs broken: "compelled ..., had them condemned" lacks a coordinating "and".
replacement: Afterwards Brasidas let the allies go home and went back himself to Corinth, to prepare for his expedition to Thrace, his original destination. The Athenians also returned home. The Megarians in the city who were most implicated in the Athenian negotiation knew that they had been detected, and presently disappeared. The rest conferred with the friends of the exiles and restored the party at Pegae, after binding them under solemn oaths to take no vengeance for the past and only to consult the real interests of the town. However, as soon as these men were in office, they held a review of the heavy infantry. They separated the battalions and picked out about a hundred of their enemies, those thought to be most involved in the correspondence with the Athenians. They brought them before the people and compelled the vote to be given openly, and had them condemned and executed, and established a close oligarchy in the town. This revolution lasted a very long while, although effected by a very few partisans.
